home.problemTitle: Why do most people fail at English?
home.problemSub: Not for lack of information — the internet is full of it. They fail because of this:

problems.title: Scattered tricks
problems.desc: You learn lots of things with no system, so the effort never compounds into fluency.

problems.title: No real speaking
problems.desc: You understand shows but freeze when you speak — because you never practiced speaking.

problems.title: No accountability
problems.desc: You start motivated and quit after two weeks. Inconsistency is the real problem.

home.systemSub: Six pillars grounded in language-acquisition science — working together to actually get you there.

pillars.title: Comprehensible input
pillars.desc: You hear and understand English at your level, building natural intuition.

pillars.title: Speaking + feedback
pillars.desc: You speak from day one and get gentle correction — that's what builds fluency and confidence.

pillars.title: Accent Lab
pillars.desc: Pronunciation training for the exact sounds Arabic speakers get wrong (like school, not iskool).

pillars.title: Spaced review
pillars.desc: We revisit everything over time so it sticks and you don't forget.

pillars.title: Mindset & discipline
pillars.desc: The habits and consistency that get you there — part of the curriculum, not a pep talk.

pillars.title: Community & accountability
pillars.desc: A group moving with you and checking on you daily, so you actually finish.

home.outcomeDesc: After ~12 weeks of consistent effort, you can hold a simple English conversation with confidence — introduce yourself, your family, your day, order something, give directions — with a clearer accent, and you'll have a before/after video proving the difference.

accentLab.title: Accent Lab — the sounds Arabic speakers get wrong
accentLab.sub: Pronunciation training built for Arabic speakers. These are the most common recurring errors — and all of them are fixable.
accentLab.intro: Arabic doesn't have some of the sounds English has, so our brain swaps them for the closest Arabic sound. The result is predictable errors we can fix precisely.

sounds.title: school, not iskool
sounds.desc: Consonant clusters — glide through them without inserting an extra vowel.

sounds.title: job, not gob
sounds.desc: The /dʒ/ sound — as Egyptians we say jim as /g/, so we must train the 'j'.

sounds.title: people, not beople
sounds.desc: The /p/ sound — lips together + a puff of air.

sounds.title: very, not fery
sounds.desc: The /v/ sound — top teeth on your lower lip + voice.

sounds.title: think, not sink
sounds.desc: The /θ/ sound — tongue tip lightly between your teeth.

guide.title: Your free guide: the 5 sounds Arabic speakers get wrong
guide.sub: Apply these and your English gets clearer right away. You won't be native in a day — but this is a real first step.
guide.intro: Arabic lacks some English sounds, so our brain swaps them for the closest Arabic sound. The result is predictable errors we can fix precisely.
guide.soundsTitle: The 5 sounds — and how to fix them

sounds.title: school, not iskool
sounds.fix: Glide through consonant clusters without inserting an extra vowel.

sounds.title: job, not gob
sounds.fix: The /dʒ/ sound = d + j together — not the Egyptian /g/.

sounds.title: people, not beople
sounds.fix: The /p/ sound = lips together + a puff of air (try a paper in front of your mouth).

sounds.title: very, not fery
sounds.fix: The /v/ sound = top teeth on your lower lip + voice.

sounds.title: think, not sink
sounds.fix: The /θ/ sound = tongue tip lightly between your teeth.

plan: Day 1: consonant clusters — record: school, street, desk.
Day 5: /θ/ — record: think, three, this — then re-record Day 1 and hear the difference.

about.title: The EEC Story
about.sub: Not just a course — a system I built from my real journey.
story: I'm an Egyptian who reached a near-native level in English — not by luck, by discipline.
A strong grammar foundation from a young age, and a full university education in English (Faculty of Commerce, English).
And 6 years in Dubai speaking English every day with people from over 200 nationalities.
I built the system I wish I'd had when I started — and now I teach it to Arabic speakers who want to get there.
